claim: In a double-blind placebo-controlled study with N=480 males in an Intergroup Attacker-Defender contest game, oxytocin reduced contributions to attack.
source: In a double-blind placebo-controlled study with N=480 males in an Intergroup Attacker-Defender contest game, we found that oxytocin reduced contributions to attack and over time increased attacker's within-group coordination of contributions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study described.

claim: Oxytocin increased attacker's within-group coordination of contributions over time.

claim: Attackers given oxytocin better tracked their rival's historical defense.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous scholarly work.

claim: Out-group hostility and aggression serves to defend the in-group against hostility from neighboring groups.

claim: Individuals are more strongly motivated to contribute to defend one's own group than to attack out-groups.
source: Recent work has showed that individuals are more strongly motivated to contribute to defend one's own group than to attack out-groups and, importantly, that out-group attacks frequently fail because individual contributions to out-group attacks are poorly coordinated (De Dreu et al., 2016a).

claim: Out-group attacks frequently fail because individual contributions to out-group attacks are poorly coordinated.

claim: Attacking rivals who are expected to have strong defenses more likely results in failure and waste than attacking groups expected to be weak and defenseless.

The attacker group won and took away defender group's remaining MU (spoils from winning, 60 – GDefender), which were divided equally among three attacker group members (each attacker member received: (60 – GDefender)/3) and added to their remaining endowments (20 – IAttacker-i).

claim: Attacker groups given oxytocin tracked their rival's past defense and attacked especially when defenders appeared more rather than less vulnerable.
source: Third, we examined how attacker groups collectively identified when to attack by creating a past defense parameter α (average defender group's investment in the last two rounds, that is (Dj-1+Dj-2)/2 on round j) and regressed attacker group's investments onto α (attack increased when defender groups were vulnerable rather than strong, as indicated by α approaching -1). It showed that attacker groups given oxytocin tracked their rival's past defense and attacked especially when defenders appeared more rather than less vulnerable (i.e. attack regressed negatively on rival's historical defense).
